newsitem.title: USA: For NYSE options business, money beat location.
newsitem.headline: For NYSE options business, money beat location.

text.p: In the battle for the New York Stock Exchange's equity options business, money, money, money beat out location, location, location.
By relying on location, the American Stock Exchange lost out on its bid to secure the equity options business of the NYSE, industry sources said.
On Thursday, the NYSE's board of directors recommended the exchange negotiate the sale of its options unit to the Chicago Board Options Exchange.
CBOE president and chief operating officer Charles Henry said the exchange was pleased to have won the battle.
"We will now begin working on a mutually acceptable agreement," he said in a statement.
But up until earlier this week, the odds-on favorite to win the business was the AMEX, which had the big benefit of being only a few blocks away from the NYSE in lower Manhattan.
Traders in New York familiar with the situation said the AMEX relied too heavily on that fact and was not aggressive in its bid for the business.
"The AMEX relied upon geographic location," one trader said. "They never dreamed people would ever want to move."
But sources at the AMEX said the exchange's bid was indeed aimed at accommodating the 100 or so NYSE options floor members.

"The NYSE might not have found (the AMEX bid) as attractive as the CBOE's because there weren't as many dollar signs," one source at the AMEX said. The AMEX offer "was targeted at making the members there happy."
AMEX officials declined to comment.
Financial terms were not disclosed and industry sources gave a wide-ranging price tag from $10 million to $20 million.
Whatever the price, industry experts said the NYSE would not likely reap a big profit because the business is so small.
The NYSE is the smallest of the five U.S. options exchanges. Last year it traded 2.8 million options contracts. The CBOE, where most options are traded, trades about 180 million contracts a year.
Even so, dollars appeared to be the swing factor.
"I think it was money," said Michael Schwartz at Oppenheimer & Co.
"On a campatibility basis, the AMEX system, being specialist-based, would have made for a more transparent transfer," Schwartz said.
Traders said while the majority of the NYSE options floor members would have preferred to stay on the East Coast, they were generally pleased with the CBOE's bid.
"Across the board people would have rather stayed, but when you compare the bids side by side" the CBOE's bid was better, one trader in New York said.
Details of the various bids, which also came from the Philadelphia Stock Exchange, Pacific Stock Exchange and New York Cotton Exchange, were not available.
But traders said the CBOE's bid included new floor space for the New York traders and better seat deals than the AMEX bid.
